newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Northwest hydropower dam releases rise.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Northwest hydropower dam releases rise.

text.p: Hydroelectric dams in the Pacific Northwest are releasing extra water to clear reservoir space for much higher than normal spring runoff, regional officials said Friday.
"We are drafting the system for flood control purposes," said Cindy Henriksen, chief of the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers reservoir control center in Portland, Oregon.
Although water storage targets vary throughout the system, most projects are draining at rates that are causing significant spill because "there is more water than powerhouse capacity," she said.
A spokesman for Idaho Power Co said outflow from the utility's Brownlee reservoir on the Snake River is spilt about even between spill and flows through power turbines.
Brownlee is being drafted to its minimum flood target of 1,976 feet by the end of April, compared with a bottom of 2,017 feet last year, Henriksen said.
"This year most of the snowpack is above the Brownlee project," where spring runoff is forecast at 177 percent of normal, she noted.

Nevertheless, reservoir storage is being cleared throughout the hydropower system on the Snake and Columbia rivers with the aim of regulating outflow from The Dalles dam in Oregon if the Portland area is threatened with flooding.
The Northwest River Forecast Center last estimated runoff at The Dalles at 137 percent of average for January-July.

Henriksen at the Corps of Engineers said minimum flood control levels for the hydropower system could be reduced even further if that runoff rate is confirmed when the center releases its early February forecast.
The February update of the forecast is expected later Friday.
